summary: Georgia lies at the southern foot of the Caucasus Mountains, has an eight-thousand-year history of winemaking, and was one of the first countries to make Christianity its state religion.

ranking.name: Georgian Orthodox Church
ranking.description: In the early 4th century, Saint Nino, a female missionary said to have come from Cappadocia, converted King Mirian III of the Kingdom of Iberia (eastern Georgia) to Christianity, making Georgia one of the world's earliest Christian countries. In the Middle Ages the Georgian Church gained autocephalous status, and, sandwiched between the two great Islamic empires of Persia and the Ottomans, Orthodoxy became the core of national identity. In 1811 the Russian Empire abolished its autocephaly, and it was suppressed again in the Soviet period; after independence in 1991 the church revived rapidly, and Patriarch Ilia II, in office since 1977, was one of the most trusted figures in the country.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Georgia's Muslims fall mainly into two groups: the Azerbaijanis of the Kvemo Kartli region in the south, who are Shia, which is related to the influence of Safavid Persia since the Middle Ages; and the Georgians of Adjara in the south-west, who converted to Sunni Islam under Ottoman rule after the 16th century and were not incorporated into Russia until 1878. In addition, the Kists of the Pankisi Gorge in the north-east are also Muslims.

ranking.name: Armenian Apostolic Church
ranking.description: Armenians have lived in Georgia for a long time, and in the 19th century they made up a high proportion of the merchants and middle class of the capital Tbilisi. After the Russo-Turkish War of 1828–1829, large numbers of Armenians moved from the area around Erzurum in the Ottoman Empire into the Javakheti region in the south, and today's followers of the Armenian Apostolic Church are concentrated there and in Tbilisi.

religion.background: Georgia accepted Christianity in the 4th century, and the distinctive Georgian Orthodox Church reached its peak in the medieval Golden Age (the time of David IV and Queen Tamar, 11th–13th centuries), when many monasteries were built. Later invasions by Persians, Ottomans and Mongols brought Islamic influence, leading regions such as Adjara to convert to Islam. From 1801 the Russian Empire annexed Georgia and the church was absorbed into the Russian Orthodox system, and it was further persecuted in the Soviet period. After independence in 1991, Orthodoxy revived rapidly and plays a central role in national identity.

language.official: Georgian is the official language, and Abkhaz also has official status in the Abkhazia region.

ranking.name: Georgian
ranking.description: Georgian belongs to the Kartvelian language family and is unrelated to the surrounding Indo-European and Turkic languages; it has its own unique alphabet, and the earliest firmly dated inscriptions go back to the 5th century. The 12th-century poet Rustaveli's epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin is regarded as the summit of Georgian literature. In 1978 the Soviet authorities tried to remove Georgian's status as the state language from the constitution, which provoked large protests in the capital and was withdrawn, so April 14 became "Mother Language Day".

ranking.name: Azerbaijani
ranking.description: Azerbaijani belongs to the Turkic language family and is spoken mainly in the Kvemo Kartli region in the south-east, where the ancestors of the local Azerbaijanis have settled since the Middle Ages. Many residents of Azerbaijani origin do not speak Georgian well, and since 2010 the government has promoted special quotas for university admission and language courses to help them integrate into society.

ranking.name: Armenian
ranking.description: Armenian is spoken mainly in the Samtskhe-Javakheti region in the south and in the capital Tbilisi; in the early 19th century large numbers of Armenians moved in from the Ottoman Empire, forming areas with an Armenian majority, and local schools still teach in Armenian today.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: After Georgia was annexed to the Russian Empire in 1801, Russian became the administrative language, and in the Soviet period it was the inter-ethnic lingua franca and a necessary language for further education and employment. After independence in 1991, and especially after the Russo-Georgian War of 2008, the status of Russian declined, schools made English the first foreign language, and only a minority now have Russian as their mother tongue.

language.history: Georgian is one of the oldest written languages of the Caucasus region; tradition holds that the alphabet was created by King Parnavaz in the 3rd century BC, while the earliest surviving inscriptions date from the 5th century. In the Middle Ages Georgian developed a rich literature along with the church and the kingdom. After annexation by the Russian Empire in the 19th century Russian became the official language, but Georgian intellectuals promoted the preservation of the language. In the Soviet period Georgian kept the status of a union republic language, the 1978 protests successfully defended its constitutional status, and after independence in 1991 it became the sole state language.

ranking.name: Khachapuri
ranking.description: Bread baked from fermented dough filled with plenty of salty cheese; the Adjarian version is shaped like a boat, with a raw egg yolk and butter placed in the center and mixed in when eating.
ranking.history: The name is made up of the Georgian "khacho" (curd cheese) and "puri" (bread), and it is Georgia's most representative food. Different regions developed different shapes: the round loaf of Imereti, the double-layered cheese bread of Megrelia, and the boat-like form of the Adjara region on the Black Sea coast, said to symbolize a ship and the sun. In 2019 khachapuri was listed as Georgia's national intangible cultural heritage, and Georgia even has a "khachapuri index" that measures prices by its cost.

ranking.name: Khinkali
ranking.description: Thick dough wrapped around spiced minced pork and beef with broth, pinched into many pleats and boiled; when eating, one first sips the broth and then bites into the meat filling.
ranking.history: Khinkali originated in the mountain areas of north-eastern Georgia, such as Pshavi, Khevsureti and Tusheti, where herders made it with mutton. It is generally thought that this kind of filled dumpling may be related to the dumpling tradition brought by the Mongol westward campaigns of the 13th century. Georgians eat khinkali by holding the knot of dough at the top in the hand, first biting a small hole to sip the broth; the knot is usually not eaten but left on the plate to count how many were eaten. It is a classic dish for Georgian gatherings and for drinking wine.

ranking.name: Churchkhela
ranking.description: Walnuts strung on a long thread are repeatedly dipped into a thick syrup boiled from grape juice and flour, and air-dried to become a long candle-like sweet.
ranking.history: Georgia is one of the world's oldest wine-producing regions; archaeological finds show that its winemaking history goes back about eight thousand years, and the technique of making wine in clay vessels (qvevri) has been listed as UNESCO intangible cultural heritage. Churchkhela is made from grape juice during the autumn grape harvest festival (Rtveli); it is nutritious and keeps well, and traditionally soldiers and travelers carried it as an energy food. Today it is an essential sweet at New Year and festivals, and a favorite souvenir of tourists.

ranking.name: Pkhali
ranking.description: Vegetables such as spinach, beets, beans or cabbage are chopped and mixed with walnut paste, garlic and herbs, formed into small balls and garnished with pomegranate seeds.
ranking.history: Walnuts are widely grown in Georgia and are the core ingredient of many dishes. In the Georgian Orthodox fasting periods and on every Wednesday and Friday, animal products may not be eaten, so a rich range of cold vegetarian dishes made with vegetables and walnuts developed, of which pkhali is representative. It often appears as an opening cold dish at the traditional Georgian feast, the supra, and is enjoyed with Georgian wine.

ranking.name: Satsivi (chicken in walnut sauce)
ranking.description: Boiled chicken or turkey is soaked in a thick white sauce made with walnuts, garlic and spices such as blue fenugreek, and eaten chilled.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Georgian "tsivi", meaning "cold", because the dish is usually eaten cold. The spices used in it, such as blue fenugreek and marigold, reflect Georgia's position at the meeting point of the Silk Road and Caucasus trade. It is an indispensable dish at Georgian New Year and Christmas feasts, traditionally made with turkey, symbolizing the abundance of the festival.
